earlier_scan.source_named: Elias, Alexander (2018) MA thesis, Leiden, on Central Flores languages (pp.126-147 cover Nage per Glottolog); repository copy not located without search.
earlier_scan.note: Central Flores languages are typically described with penultimate stress; verify in Elias 2018 when reachable.

sources.citation: Baird, Louise. 2002. A grammar of Keo: an Austronesian language of East Nusantara. PhD thesis, Australian National University, 329 pp. hdl:1885/9446.
sources.note: Sec. 2.6 Stress p.53 (p.49) is about Keo, not Nage: 'Stress in Keo is predictable: it typically falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. The exception to this is in disyllabic words in which there is a schwa in the first syllable, in which case stress falls on the ultimate syllable.' Nage is mentioned only in sec. 1.2.4 ('Charles Grimes et al. (1997) treat Nage and Keo as a single language') and sec. 1.6 (Forth 1994a,b and Tule 2001 argue Nage and Keo are separate ethnic groups). No Nage stress statement.

sources.citation: Elias, Alexander. 2020. Are the Central Flores languages really typologically unusual? eScholarship preprint qt5p49t2w2 (published in Gil & Schapper eds., Austronesian Undressed, Benjamins 2020, pp.287-338, DOI 10.1075/tsl.129).
sources.note: No stress statement. p.16: 'Nage has not received much attention from linguists specifically, but Nage culture and folk classification has been the subject of numerous publications by the anthropologist Gregory Forth (Forth 1998, 2004, 2008, 2009, 2016).'

sources.citation: Elias, Alexander. 2018. Lio and the Central Flores languages. Research MA thesis, Leiden University, 238 pp. hdl:1887/69452 (Glottolog ref 570997; listed by Glottolog as a phonology/comparative).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Sec. 2.6 Stress (p.61, p.64) is about Lio only: 'Stress has a low functional load in Lio and is usually initial in isolated words'. Nage appears in sec. 3.3.1 (pp.77-79: Eastern Nage/Nangamboa and Central Nage/Boawae consonant inventories, Central Nage data taken from Baird 2002) and in the comparative chapters (pp.126-147); a full-text search for stress/accent the whole text for stress/accent/penult finds no statement about Nage. p.78: 'Very little linguistic work has been carried out on Nage.. a dialect survey of Nage is crucial.. but remains to be carried out.'

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page nage1237 (refs: Elias 2018 pp.126-147, Baird 2002, Ethnologue 2025; Glottolog's most extensive descriptions: Pita 2016, Forth 2004, Pita 1984, Forth 1981, HRAF 1972).
sources.note: Nothing; confirms that the only 'phonology'-typed description is Pita 2016 and that nage1237 has 3 dialect children (names not extracted).

sources.citation: Forth, Gregory. 2009. Human beings and other people: classification of human groups and categories among the Nage of Flores (eastern Indonesia). Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 165(4): 493-514.

sources.citation: Forth, Gregory. 1998. Things that go po in the night: the classification of birds, sounds, and spirits among the Nage of eastern Indonesia. Journal of Ethnobiology 18(2): 189-209.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or pronunciation (a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/orthography yields only non-linguistic uses of 'stress').

sources.citation: Forth, Gregory. 1995. Ethnozoological classification and classificatory language among the Nage of eastern Indonesia. Journal of Ethnobiology 15(1): 45-69.
sources.note: Note 1 (pp.65-66) gives only orthographic conventions (bh/dh implosives, gh fricative, glottal stop phonemic initially and medially, schwa vs long e marked with acute accent); nothing about stress.
